title: Indian Students Cool on the American Dream as Europe Emerges as the New Promised Land
excerpt: Tighter US visa rules and the India-EU trade deal are driving a generational shift in where young Indians choose to study, with European enrolments climbing and consultants reporting a 25-30% surge in inquiries.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's overseas student outflow dropped to 626,000 in 2025 from over 908,000 in 2023.
  • The India-EU trade deal facilitates easier visa routes and qualification recognition for Indian students.
  • European tuition fees are 50-80% lower than in the US, attracting more Indian students.
  • Indian enrolment in the Netherlands rose to 3,700 in 2025-26, up from 2,630 in 2018-19.
  • Education inquiries for Europe surged by 25-30% since the trade deal was signed.

  • India's overseas student outflow fell to 626,000 in 2025 from over 908,000 in 2023 as tighter US visa rules and rising costs deter applicants
  • The India-EU trade deal signed in January 2026 creates structured pathways for Indian students and workers, with easier visa routes and improved qualification recognition
  • European tuition fees are 50-80% lower than in the US, and education consultants report a 25-30% jump in inquiries since the deal
  • More than 121,000 Indians already study in the EU, about half the US total, but the gap is narrowing as enrolments climb across the continent

A Chennai Graduate Breaks With Family Tradition

A. Shrinikheathan, a 22-year-old engineering graduate from Chennai, is learning German and preparing for a language proficiency test as he applies for a master's degree in Germany. He is breaking from his family's long tradition of studying in the United States.

"The world is becoming more multi-polar. Earlier, the U.S. was all that everyone was talking about," Shrinikheathan told Reuters, adding he was happy to have study choices beyond the "wildly more expensive" United States and Canada.

"He is breaking from his family's long tradition of studying in the United States.</p> <p>"The world is becoming more multi-polar."

His decision is part of a broader shift. Young Indians are increasingly looking to Europe as Washington tightens immigration controls and the European Union rolls out the red carpet for Indian talent. A dozen students and education consultants told Reuters the shift is real and accelerating.

The Numbers Tell the Story

India's overseas student outflow fell to about 626,000 in 2025 from more than 908,000 in 2023, according to government data. Students have grown wary of tougher visa rules and rising costs in the US and other traditional destinations like Australia and the UK. Last week, Washington moved to cap foreign student visas at four years as part of its sweeping immigration crackdown.

Meanwhile, Indian interest in Europe has surged since the India-EU trade deal signed in January 2026. The agreement creates structured pathways for students and skilled workers through easier visa routes, clearer post-study work options, and improved recognition of Indian qualifications.

"For the first time, a major economic bloc is saying, 'We want Indian talent at scale,'" said Arnav Kumar, co-founder of study-abroad platform Leap, who forecasts a 60-70% jump in student and worker flows over three to five years.

Europe's Cost Advantage

European tuition fees are typically 50-80% lower than those in the US, according to education consultant KC Overseas, with lower living costs further reducing the bill. For middle-class Indian families already spending $3.7 billion annually on overseas education, the arithmetic is shifting decisively.

Students are increasingly matching destinations to career goals: Germany for engineering, the Netherlands for work-life balance, Portugal for affordable postgraduate research, and France for management programmes. The growing number of English-language postgraduate programmes and the prospect of greater mobility across the 27-nation bloc are additional draws.

— EU Official, statement to Reuters

Early Data Signals a Real Shift

Indian enrolment in the Netherlands climbed to about 3,700 in 2025-26 from 2,630 in 2018-19, making Indians the third-largest non-EU student group, according to Statistics Netherlands. Eindhoven University of Technology reported about 2,140 pre-enrolments from India for the coming academic year, up from roughly 1,390 a year earlier.

Leiden University's Indian intake in regular master's programmes jumped to 120 this year from 70 in 2021. Italy's Padua University said partner agencies in India were reporting rising interest in Europe, including from regions that traditionally sent students to the United States.

Education consultancy Europe Study Centre has seen inquiries jump 25-30% since the trade deal, with director Sivaraman Pandian calling Europe the "red-hot destination" for families put off by rising costs and tougher visa rules elsewhere.

Challenges Remain

The path to Europe is not without hurdles. Several students pointed to language barriers, housing shortages in cities like Amsterdam, intense competition for jobs, and the need for specialised skills. Some acknowledged concerns about the rise of far-right political parties and hardening attitudes towards foreigners in parts of Europe.

"If somebody says you will get a job in this country, don't blindly believe it. Just because you studied in that country, it does not entitle you to get a job," cautioned Pandian. "You study, and you develop a skill-set; your doors are open."

Looking Ahead

If sustained, the shift could reshape global student flows, with Europe emerging as a genuine rival to North America. Whether the surge in interest translates into sustained enrolments will depend on how smoothly the India-EU agreement is implemented. But perceptions are already changing.

Chennai-based engineer T. Suthir, who is exploring colleges in the Czech Republic and Italy, put it simply: "Earlier, before the deal was finalised, my family was saying Europe is not good. Now, they are saying it's good."
